newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serbian police, protestors play cat-and-mouse game.
newsitem.headline: Serbian police, protestors play cat-and-mouse game.

text.p: Police and demonstrators played a cat-and-mouse game in the streets of the Serbian capital Belgrade on Friday as signs of autocratic President Slobodan Milosevic's authority faltering appeared to increase.
Several hundred anti-riot police threw a succession of cordons across city streets in an attempt to channel tens of thousands of pro-democracy marchers into a central square.
Witnesses said police were only partially successful in stamping their will on the proceedings.
In one instance, double lines of police gave way simply under the sheer weight of numbers after trying to restrict the demonstrators to pavements or a single lane of the road.

As cheerful, noisy contingents of opposition coalition supporters steadily converged on Republic Square after dark, one marcher said to a police officer: "The guy who told you to do this must be very clever."
The policeman smiled. "He's a real genius," he replied.
An independent radio station said one group of opposition supporters had passed no fewer than 11 police cordons en route to the square.
Earlier during the 76th day of street protests demanding acceptance of the opposition's victories in local elctions last November 17, one of Milosevic's old associates broke ranks.

Borisov Jovic, a former Yugoslav federal president who fell out with Milosevic over the rising power of the Serbian leader's wife, told a British newspaper the policy of ignoring election results had divided and weakened the government.
"If someone thinks they can do anything against...the constitution and the law, that is a very serious situation," Jovic said in the Belgrade interview.
He was quoted by the Guardian as urging Milosevic to admit election defeats and reduce the clout of his wife Mira Markovic, who heads one of the governing parties, the Yugoslav United Left.

Markovic, who among opposition activists is the most despised figure in Serbia's ruling circle, lambasted the opposition on Friday, accusing them in her regular magazine column of disrupting ordinary life and undermining the economy.

Signs of dwindling state authority have grown steadily during the marathon protests, with lawyers going on strike, teachers picketing and Belgrade university deans breaking off contacts with the pro-Milosevic rector who has resisted student demands to quit.

Three hundred members of the Belgrade Bar Association rallied on Friday to demand the resignation of the justice and interior ministers for their role in frustrating opposition efforts to have the November election results reinstated.
In another sign of dissent, the ruling Socialist Party leadership in Pirot criticised one of its own members whose ballot enabled an opposition leader to be elected mayor of the southern town.

Results of an independent opinion poll published on Friday showed that 12 percent of all Serbians over 18 years old, or roughly 700,000 people, were demonstrating on average every day across the country.
The poll, released by the Institute for Social Sciences, also found that the number of voters backing Milosevic's coalition had shrunk by one third since November.
The socialist authorities have threatened to withhold state cash from universities and schools as long as protests last, but there is no sign that this has dented opposition ardour.
In another development, the mainstream political leader of ethnic Albanians in the Serbian-ruled province of Kosovo said 37 Albanians had been arrested so far this week.

Ibrahim Rugova, head of the Democratic League of Kosovo, said the arrests were a "major provocation" by Serbian authorities in a region seen as a potential flashpoint since Milosevic cancelled its autonomy in 1989.

In Rome, the international community's High Representative for Bosnia, Carl Bildt, said Serbia was becoming the "sick man of Europe" with no way out of desperate economic straits unless Milosevic honoured the opposition's election gains.
